en: Throughout the whole wide world,
He truly made my father great.
This lord Bakai, the saint,
Is the elder left from my father, Khan Manas.
His name is known among the people;
He is a saint, a mighty conquering lord.
When storms come, no wind reaches you:
Bakai is a sheltered woodland, a dense forest.
If one had met Bakai at twenty,
Against those eighteen thousand worlds
He alone was a lion of equal worth.
What my mother Kanykei told me
Was speech without a single fault.
My uncle, Khan Bakai the lord—
Out on the open plain, the one God
Had chosen this time for us to meet.
He is my father's very dark eye.
My father who went to the Last Judgment—
My word, this is his very friend.
Once God had granted him his wish,
Your uncle, leopard Bakai's
Long-awaited one had come.
All his grief, ah, scattered;
All his pent-up sorrow opened out.
What he had lost was gathered;
Bakai's grieving soul rejoiced.
Such was Bakai, the noble lion,
The noble hero come to fifteen.
He taught what was not known,
That learned elder Bakai;
He made one sense what was not sensed,
That falcon elder Bakai.
The orphan he desired had arrived;
The Almighty truly granted him.
The sign that he had granted it:
Kökcholok beneath his saddle—
No wind could catch his trotting,
No beast could match his walking.
When he entered a descent,
His forelegs thrust like a roe deer's.
When he started climbing up,
His mane and tail streamed out.
He gnawed upon his bit,
And tore up where he trod.
The black steel bit
Clattered in his gullet,
His hooves beat on the ground.
His mouth gaped like a yawning maw;
White foam mixed with blood
Splashed upon his breast.
When orphan Semetey arrived,
Khan Bakai's Kökcholok,
Though a beast, rejoiced.
Kökcholok, the horse he rode,
Turned playful, frisking lightly;
In places Kökcholok
Played and swayed along.
Hero Bakai rode upon him,
With Semetey following.
Riding on, Bakai spoke,
Saying, “My sovereign orphan:
Stay the night and know the hospitality;
Hear the story from Bakai.
When sovereign Manas lived,
I too, my dear soul, was a sovereign,
As we raided all the peoples.
Valiant Manas then was there.
When a fearsome foe came facing us,
Of the people on the earth,
Those wicked men with black intent—
When we faced them and raided their camp,
We would plunder all their goods.
Courser Manas then was there;
We would firmly quell the rebels.
Vast treasures, yellow gold—
Gathering treasure, being khan—
My lord, alas, was laid low.
My pit was dug deep,
God boiled my bitter fate.
When your khan father passed away,
These six vile ones standing here
Brought their wicked deeds into the open.
They plundered my possessions,
And thus brought all my laughter to an end.
Sixty thousand horses on the hills,
Thoroughbreds and coursers mingled—
When the six vile ones raided,
My poor soul was thrown into distress.
Ah, my darling orphan,
I had no courser left to catch and ride,
No kinsman to lend me support.
Your father was a peerless lion;
The noble hero passed away.
When bloodthirsty Manas died,
When this soul came to know grief,
Countless treasures, ample wealth—
When my poor soul beheld them,
Those coarse dogs measured by the whip,
And divided them in wild confusion.
They dug my pit deep,
And thus boiled my bitter fate.
Kanykei, who supported me,
And Semetey, left by my Khan Manas,
Fled away to seek a refuge.
When black-faced Kanykei had fled,
Abyke, Köbösh, those six vile ones—
There was no one to support me.
They heaped turmoil, embers on my head,
And fired their shots like rain.
Your father's grave! The world is shit!
The six vile ones would not greet me,
And made your uncle pale with fear.
“I will cut off his beard,” they said,
“Seize bloodthirsty Bakai,
And offer him in sacrifice.”
The reason they behaved this way:
Khan Tekechi and Khan Shygai
Laid a claim against my poor soul.
They stood at Üyrülmö,
And held a council for three days.
They readied spears and gathered shot;
The six vile ones came out to fight,
And battled your uncle, Khan Bakai.
The forty companions left by Manas,
With Kyrgylchal, the dog of them all—
Like stars streaming from the sky,
They joined those six vile ones.
They drew their bows like falling rain,
And fired their shots like hail.
When the dogs came to besiege me,
My wide possessions were divided,
My treasury was left strewn out.
My ribs came loose and split apart;
My strength was torn in all directions.
Utterly alone, a solitary pine,
With no one to support me—
I, the childless leopard, was alone.
Surviving without dying,
For forty days and nights
I fought those vile men.
Cursed be loneliness!
No forest I could flee into,
No place in which to hide,
No people to support me,
No great Kyrgyz nation at my side.
From tamarisk-grown Keng-Kol and great Talas,
Many Kyrgyz, frightened off,
Moved and settled at Ürbüs.
They said, “Bakai has become a raider,”
And I acquired an evil name.
Five hundred households remained,
At Bek-Jailoo, above Besh-Tash,
I, Bakai, remained in hiding.
A great dispute arose and tangled us;
My poor soul fought those six vile ones,
Exchanging fire for twelve years.
I let no soul ascend Besh-Tash,
Broke up its entrance and held a fort,
Held it firmly, letting no one pass.
As I persisted in defiance,
Some sixty champions of Abyke
I shot down by myself.
I climbed to a strong place and settled;
I earned the name of troublemaker,
And acquired an evil name.
Drinking blood, I hardened myself.
Among the many Kyrgyz and Argyn,
I was called Bakai the fugitive.
I slaughtered kin and drank their blood;
I, upright Bakai, drank poison.
Not a soul came to visit,
And I lacked strength against the vile ones.
The young falcon went back to its place,
The wanderer back to his camp;
The harrier went back to its place,
The mixed folk back to their camps.
My poor soul stayed and endured
In the land Khan Manas had found.
Ah, the dogs! The fugitives went to their own kind.
I had no khan to support me,
No one like you, left by my Khan Manas,
No orphan bringing blessings.
Such is this world of shit!
When mountain-like Manas died,
When Bakai came to know torment,
Those coarse dogs gathered,
And raided my caravan at the ford.
From those dogs that swaggered proudly,
My foal, I still have not taken revenge.
They broke up my migration from Talas;
From those strutting slaves,
I still have not taken revenge.
No back on which to bind my belt,
No place in which to hide—
My orphan fled before he was grown.
When you went to Bukhara,
My foal, my wing lost a whole span.
The offspring of a khan's son—
Otherwise, why should he have to flee?
The hostility of dogs in the camp,
The six vile ones' lack of fellowship!
A nobleman's young camel—
Why should he have to flee away,
Carried off to Bukhara?
Such a lack of care among the people!
Now know, my foal,
The hostility of those six vile ones.
When the slaves came in a mass,
When they raided livestock without a master,
Kökcholok remained, and I remained.
My Talas stayed safe;
This soul of mine remained free.
We bound our birch-shafted spears,
And warred for twelve years.
Splitting gallbladders, cutting off heads,
We suffered great torment.
Here I, Bakai, did not die,
Nor did I see the other world.
I suffered sorrow for your sake;
Semetey, did you ever think of me?
I wasted away herding camels.
Twelve years had passed
As I wondered, ‘Will my orphan come?’
And burned with longing for you.
Now God has granted my wish,
And the orphan I awaited has come.
Now listen, orphan,
Lend your ear to what I know:
There is a wrong Kanykei has done,
There are wonders in many places.
My spring that feeds a valley river,
My dear one, found when I was near death,
When the possessions were scattered,
When your poor mother fled,
We would earn blame if we left without seeing it:
The treasury your mother dug
She entrusted to poor me,
And left it in my keeping.
Let us go to your treasury;
From the wealth your father left,
Let us take whatever you desire.”
So saying, Bakai sped away,
Urging his horse toward the blue cliff.
At the bubbling dark spring,
At the plane tree by the spring,
They stopped and offered prayers,
Then passed on farther.
They came to hills on hills,
To hilly passes and ridges.
Taking a shortcut on a narrow path,
And leading Semetey,
At Kapka-Tash, where treasure lay hidden,
Gold and jewels intermingled,
They now passed through Kapka-Tash.
The black cliff mottled gray—
The treasure left in trust—
